questions.prompt: Which is ∫ (6x²−4x+5) dx, where C is an arbitrary constant?
questions.explanation: Integrating term by term gives 6x³/3−4x²/2+5x+C=2x³−2x²+5x+C. The single arbitrary constant accounts for all vertical translates on the real-number interval. A: Integrate each term using the power rule and linearity. B: The linear term −4x integrates to −2x², not −4x². C: This raises powers without dividing by their new exponents. D: This differentiates the original expression rather than finding a primitive.

questions.prompt: On x>0, which is ∫ x^(−3) dx?
questions.explanation: For a power other than −1, add 1 to the exponent and divide by that new exponent. Here −3+1=−2, giving x^(−2)/(−2)+C=−1/(2x²)+C. The positive interval avoids the original pole at zero. A: This loses the sign from dividing by −2. B: The new power is −2 and dividing by it supplies the negative factor 1/2. C: This is the derivative of x^(−3), not its antiderivative. D: The logarithm rule applies to x^(−1), not x^(−3).

questions.prompt: On the interval x<0, which is ∫ 1/x dx?
questions.explanation: For x<0, |x|=−x>0. The chain rule gives d[ln(−x)]/dx=(−1)/(−x)=1/x. Thus ln|x|+C is the primitive on the specified negative interval; the real formula ln x alone would not be defined there. A: This would have derivative −1/x. B: This has derivative 1/x² rather than 1/x. C: The absolute value keeps the logarithm real and its derivative is 1/x on this interval. D: This has derivative ln|x| rather than 1/x.

questions.prompt: Angles are in radians. Which is ∫ cos x dx?
questions.explanation: An antiderivative must differentiate back to the integrand. Since d(sin x)/dx=cos x in radians, the indefinite integral is sin x+C. Retaining cosine or applying the sine derivative in reverse with the wrong sign does not work. A: This has derivative −cos x. B: This has derivative −sin x. C: This has derivative sin x. D: The derivative of sine is cosine.

questions.prompt: Which is ∫ (3 cos x−2 sin x) dx, with x in radians?
questions.explanation: Linearity gives 3∫cos x dx−2∫sin x dx. Since ∫sin x dx=−cos x+C, the result is 3 sin x+2 cos x+C. The two constants may be combined into one arbitrary constant. A: The sine contribution integrates to a positive cosine term because its derivative carries a minus. B: This differentiates to 3 cos x+2 sin x. C: This gives the wrong sign on the cosine integrand term. D: This retains the integrand rather than integrating it.

questions.prompt: On x>0, which formula is ∫ eˣ dx?
questions.explanation: Because d(eˣ)/dx=eˣ, the primitive is eˣ+C. Unlike integrating a constant, integrating a variable exponential does not mean multiplying it by x. The other formulas fail the derivative-back check. A: The product rule produces the extra term x eˣ in its derivative. B: The exponential is its own derivative and hence its own primitive. C: This differentiates to 1/x, not eˣ. D: The inner negative sign gives derivative −e^(−x).

questions.prompt: On −π/2<x<π/2, which is ∫ sec²x dx, with angles in radians?
questions.explanation: The basic derivative d(tan x)/dx=sec²x gives the primitive tan x+C. The specified interval excludes the tangent poles. A primitive for the entire interval must also be defined at zero, which cotangent is not. A: This gives derivative −sec²x. B: The secant derivative is sec x tan x, not sec²x. C: The tangent derivative is sec²x on this pole-free interval. D: The cotangent derivative is −csc²x where it is defined, and cotangent also fails at zero.

questions.prompt: Which is ∫ 1/(1+x²) dx on the real numbers?
questions.explanation: The standard derivative d(arctan x)/dx=1/(1+x²) identifies the primitive arctan x+C. The denominator is positive for all real x, so no interval split or absolute value is needed. A logarithm would require a matching numerator derivative. A: This changes the derivative sign. B: Its derivative has the extra numerator factor 2x. C: The quotient derivative is (1−x²)/(1+x²)². D: The inverse-tangent derivative matches the entire reciprocal quadratic.

The basic inverse-sine derivative is 1/√(1−x²) on (−1,1). Therefore arcsin x+C is the primitive. The endpoints are excluded because the integrand denominator vanishes there; no claim of a finite endpoint derivative is made. A: The principal inverse-sine derivative matches the positive radical reciprocal. B: This gives the negative of the required derivative. C: This has derivative 1/(1+x²), a different denominator. D: This has derivative −x/√(1−x²), with an extra numerator.

questions.prompt: Which describes all antiderivatives of the zero function on the real numbers?
options: F(x)=C, where C is any real constant.
questions.explanation: An antiderivative F must satisfy F′=0 everywhere. Every constant F=C works. Conversely, for any a<b the Mean Value Theorem gives F(b)−F(a)=F′(c)(b−a)=0, so F cannot vary. Thus the complete family is precisely the constant functions. A: Zero is one valid constant, but it is not the only one. B: Every constant has zero derivative, and the Mean Value Theorem excludes nonconstant primitives. C: One is another valid constant, but all real constants are allowed. D: This family generally has derivative C rather than zero.

questions.prompt: For F′(x)=1/x on the disconnected domain x≠0, which statement about antiderivative constants is correct?
options: The additive constants must be the same on both intervals.
No antiderivative exists on either interval.
The intervals x<0 and x>0 may have independent additive constants.
An arbitrary nonconstant function of x may replace the constant on either interval.
questions.explanation: On each connected interval, primitives have the form ln|x| plus a constant. A derivative equation on x≠0 imposes no matching condition across the excluded zero. The negative and positive sides may therefore use different constants, each fixed within its own interval. A: That conclusion requires one connected interval spanning both points, which this domain lacks. B: The function ln|x| differentiates to 1/x on each interval. C: Zero is excluded, so there is no condition joining the two separate interval primitives. D: Such an addition would generally change the derivative.
